paper.title: WebGPT: Browser-Assisted Question-Answering with Human Feedback

read_sources.note: Used for arXiv metadata, abstract, author list, and revision history.
Read for browser environment design, data collection, training methods, ELI5 and TruthfulQA results, scaling analysis, and web-access risks.
Used for public project framing, result summary, citation/evaluation caveats, and deployment risk discussion.

summary.one_sentence: WebGPT trains GPT-3 to answer long-form questions by operating a text browser, collecting citations, and optimizing answer quality with human feedback.
summary.thesis: The paper's lasting contribution is the environment framing: make web research a human-demonstrable action loop, then train a model to imitate and improve that loop with preferences.
summary.why_it_matters: WebGPT predates most agent frameworks but already has the shape of a serious agent: a constrained tool interface, trajectory demonstrations, preference optimization, citations for audit, and a threat model for side effects.

prior_state: Long-form QA systems needed both retrieval and synthesis, and prior methods often optimized document retrieval separately from answer quality.
Language models hallucinated obscure factual claims because pretraining alone did not force grounding in current sources.
Human evaluation of factual accuracy is hard when model answers do not expose the evidence behind their claims.
Browser-use models needed a task setup humans could perform so demonstrations and comparisons could be collected.
problem.key_gap: The paper asks how to train a language model to use a web browser for open-ended QA and make factuality evaluation tractable through collected references.
assumptions: A text-only browser action space is expressive enough for ELI5-style web research.
Human browsing demonstrations teach the model the browser protocol and research loop.
References collected during browsing make human preference and factuality judgments easier.
Reward models can rank cited long-form answers well enough to guide rejection sampling or RL.

concepts.name: Text-based browser
concepts.definition: A constrained browsing environment exposing search, click, find, quote, scroll, back, top, and end commands to the model.

concepts.name: Reference collection
concepts.definition: The model quotes extracts from visited pages, storing title, domain, and passage as evidence for the final answer.

concepts.name: Behavior cloning
concepts.definition: Supervised fine-tuning on human demonstrations of using the browser to answer questions.

concepts.name: Best-of-n rejection sampling
concepts.definition: Sampling multiple answers and selecting the one scored highest by the reward model, trading inference-time compute for quality.

concepts.name: Reference cherry-picking
concepts.definition: A failure mode where the model selects sources that look convincing to evaluators rather than sources that fairly represent the evidence.

method.core_idea: Expose a restricted text browser to GPT-3, collect human browsing demonstrations and answer comparisons on ELI5 questions, train with behavior cloning and reward modeling, then use best-of-n rejection sampling or PPO to optimize answer quality.
action_grammar: Search <query>: send a query to Bing and display search results.
Clicked on link <id>: follow a search result or page link.
Find in page: <text>: locate text on the current page.
Quote: <text>: store a passage as a reference for the final answer.
Scrolled down/up <n>: move through the current page.
Back or Top: navigate browser state.
End: Answer: stop browsing and compose the cited final answer.
End: Nonsense or Controversial: stop without answering when appropriate.
steps: Represent browser state as text: question, page title, visible page text, cursor state, prior actions, and action budget.
Collect human demonstrations of using the browser to answer long-form ELI5 questions.
Collect human comparisons between two model-generated cited answers.
Fine-tune GPT-3 with behavior cloning on browser-command demonstrations.
Train reward models from answer comparisons.
Optimize with PPO or, for the best reported model, sample many behavior-cloned answers and select the reward-model winner.
Evaluate against human demonstrators, ELI5 reference answers, and TruthfulQA.

claims.statement: WebGPT turns web research into a constrained text-browser action loop that both humans and models can operate.
caveats: The environment depends on Bing search and a restricted, non-form-filling web interface.

claims.statement: The paper collects human demonstrations and model-output comparisons, mostly on ELI5, to train browser use and answer preference.
caveats: The task distribution is long-form Reddit QA, not arbitrary web tasks.

claims.statement: The best reported WebGPT model uses behavior cloning followed by reward-model best-of-n rejection sampling rather than PPO alone.
caveats: Best-of-n spends more inference-time compute and relies on reward-model selection quality.

claims.statement: On ELI5, the 175B best-of-64 WebGPT model is preferred to human browser demonstrators 56% of the time and to highest-voted Reddit answers 69% of the time.
caveats: The Reddit-answer comparison strips references for fairness and has blinding/style concerns discussed by the authors.

claims.statement: WebGPT improves TruthfulQA over GPT-3 but remains below human performance on out-of-distribution adversarial questions.
caveats: WebGPT answers were truncated for TruthfulQA and evaluated by humans because automated metrics were out-of-distribution.

claims.statement: Collected references make factuality evaluation more inspectable, but citations can also create overreliance and reward cherry-picked evidence.
caveats: Citations are evidence surfaces, not guarantees that the answer fairly summarizes the evidence.

claims.statement: Even restricted web access creates train-time and inference-time side-effect risks that grow with model capability.
caveats: The paper judges WebGPT's then-current side-effect risk low because actions are limited to search and following existing links.

evidence.result: The model receives a text summary of browser state and must issue one valid command: search, click, find, quote, scroll, top, back, or end. Invalid actions count against the action budget.
The authors collected around 6,000 browser demonstrations, 92% for ELI5 questions, and around 21,500 comparisons, 98% for ELI5 questions.

Training methods include behavior cloning on demonstrations, reward modeling from comparisons, PPO against the reward model with a KL penalty, and best-of-n rejection sampling against the reward model.

The main evaluated models are behavior-cloned policies with best-of-n rejection sampling: 760M best-of-4, 13B best-of-16, and 175B best-of-64. The paper reports 175B best-of-64 BC preferred 68% of the time to 175B BC, while 175B RL is preferred 58% of the time to 175B BC.
The best 175B best-of-64 model is preferred 56% of the time to human demonstrator answers and 69% of the time to highest-voted ELI5 Reddit answers.
The best model's TruthfulQA answers are true 75% of the time and both true and informative 54% of the time; all WebGPT models outperform GPT-3 prompts but remain below humans.
The paper argues references make feedback more accurate and less noisy because labelers can judge whether claims are supported by cited sources, and they make browsing trajectories inspectable.

The paper warns that citations can make answers appear more authoritative, cause overreliance, and incentivize models to cherry-pick references that persuade labelers rather than fairly represent evidence.

The authors discuss live web access risks at train and inference time, including hypothetical side effects such as editing a source to create convincing evidence, and say safety burden should rise with model capability.

agent_infra_takeaways: WebGPT is an agent paper before the term stabilized: observation, action grammar, environment transition, evidence collection, and final answer.
Tool interfaces should be constrained and logged. The text browser makes invalid actions explicit and preserves a trajectory humans can inspect.
Citations are not decoration; they are training infrastructure that lets humans evaluate factual support without doing unrestricted research from scratch.
Reward-model optimization can move from training time to inference time. Best-of-n is expensive, but effective when the environment is unpredictable.
A browser is a side-effect boundary. Even read-mostly web access creates risks once the model can search, click, and choose evidence strategically.
For agent evaluation, judge the trajectory as well as the final answer: sources, search path, quote selection, and synthesis errors are separate failure modes.
caveats: The system is trained primarily on ELI5 long-form QA, so it is not a general-purpose web automation benchmark.
The best model uses substantial inference-time compute through best-of-64 sampling.
The browser is restricted; conclusions do not directly transfer to agents with forms, authenticated sites, or write actions.
Citations can increase perceived truthfulness even when the answer is wrong or the source is unreliable.
The model can reinforce biases from GPT-3, the web, source selection, and question framing.
The paper reports out-of-distribution brittleness on TruthfulQA and examples of unreliable-source failures.

related_work.title: InstructGPT
related_work.note: InstructGPT applies the broader RLHF recipe to instruction following; WebGPT applies similar human-feedback machinery to a browser-use QA environment.

related_work.title: ReAct
related_work.note: WebGPT already has action/observation loops and evidence collection; ReAct later made reasoning/action interleaving a general prompting pattern.

related_work.title: Indirect Prompt Injection
related_work.note: WebGPT's web-reading action surface is the kind of architecture later prompt-injection work attacks when untrusted content enters the agent context.

poc.note: No PoC yet - contributions welcome. A local PoC could mock a text-browser over a small static corpus, collect quoted passages, and compare behavior cloning versus best-of-n reward selection.
